name: Islam
tagline: Submission to the one God whose final word came through Muhammad.
overview: Islam is the world's second-largest religion, founded in 7th-century Arabia through the prophethood of Muhammad. It holds that there is one God (Allah) whose final, uncreated, and verbatim revelation came through the Quran. The five pillars (declaration of faith, prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and pilgrimage) structure Muslim religious life. Islam shares with Christianity an affirmation of one personal creator God, moral law, prophetic revelation, and final judgment, but diverges sharply on the nature of Jesus, the doctrine of the Trinity, and the integrity of the biblical text.
core_claims: There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is his final messenger.
The Quran is the direct, uncreated, verbatim word of God: inerrant and unsupersedable.
Jesus (Isa) was a prophet and Messiah but not divine; he was not crucified.
The Christian and Jewish scriptures have been corrupted (tahrif) and superseded.
Salvation is by submission to God's will, good deeds, and his sovereign mercy.
christian_critique: Islam and Christianity share enough family resemblance (monotheism, prophethood, Scripture, judgment) that their differences are theologically precise rather than merely cultural. The central dispute is Christological: Islam affirms Jesus' miraculous birth and prophetic ministry but explicitly denies his crucifixion (Quran 4:157), resurrection, and divine nature. The crucifixion, however, is among the most historically secure facts of antiquity, confirmed by Tacitus, Josephus, and the Babylonian Talmud. None of whom had any motive to support Christian claims. The tahrif doctrine requires that thousands of manuscripts across multiple continents and centuries were systematically corrupted without a single trace in the textual record, a position no serious historian defends. The Trinitarian critique attacks tritheism, which Christianity itself condemned as heresy before Islam existed. The deeper question Islam cannot answer is soteriological: if Jesus was only a prophet, how are sins forgiven? Islam offers no atoning mediator, only deeds, divine mercy, and uncertainty.

articles.name: God (Allah)
articles.text: One, without partner or equal, the Creator of all. This is tawhid, the heart of Islam.

articles.name: Angels
articles.text: Created servants of God. Jibril (Gabriel) brought the revelation to Muhammad.

articles.name: Revealed books
articles.text: The Tawrat given to Moses, the Zabur to David, the Injil to Jesus, and the Quran, the final revelation, which Muslims believe God has preserved.

articles.name: Messengers
articles.text: From Adam to Muhammad, 'the seal of the prophets' (33:40). Jesus is honoured among the greatest of them.

articles.name: The Last Day
articles.text: Bodily resurrection, judgment by the weighing of deeds, then paradise or hell.

articles.name: Divine decree (qadar)
articles.text: All that happens, good and bad, happens by God's knowledge and will.

pillars.name: Shahada
pillars.text: The declaration: 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.'

pillars.name: Salah
pillars.text: Ritual prayer five times a day, facing Mecca.

pillars.name: Zakat
pillars.text: Obligatory alms, traditionally 2.5 percent of qualifying wealth each year.

pillars.name: Sawm
pillars.text: Fasting from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan.

pillars.name: Hajj
pillars.text: Pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime for those who are able.

sources.name: Quran
sources.text: 114 surahs, received by Muhammad between about 610 and 632, and standardised in writing under the caliph Uthman (ruled 644-656). For Muslims, the uncreated word of God.

sources.name: Hadith
sources.text: Reports of Muhammad's words and actions, each with a chain of narrators (isnad) and a text (matn), graded authentic (sahih), good (hasan) or weak (da'if). Sunni Islam treats the collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim as the most reliable.

sources.name: Sira
sources.text: Biography of Muhammad. The earliest, by Ibn Ishaq (died about 767), survives through later editors such as Ibn Hisham.

sources.name: Tafsir
sources.text: Commentary on the Quran. The classic works of al-Tabari (died 923) and Ibn Kathir (died 1373) remain widely used.

sources.name: Sharia and fiqh
sources.text: God's law (sharia) and the human science of working it out (fiqh), drawn from the Quran, the hadith, scholarly consensus and reasoning.

branches.name: Sunni
branches.text: About 85 to 90 percent of Muslims. Authority rests with the Quran, the example of Muhammad (sunna) and the consensus of the community.

branches.name: Shia
branches.text: About 10 to 15 percent, the largest group being Twelvers, centred on Iran and Iraq. The split began over succession: Shia Muslims hold that leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants (the imams).

branches.name: Ibadi
branches.text: A small, distinct tradition, prominent in Oman.

branches.name: Sufism
branches.text: Not a separate branch but a mystical stream found in both Sunni and Shia Islam, centred on nearness to God.

schools.name: Theology
schools.text: Ash'ari and Maturidi (the two main Sunni schools of reasoned theology), Athari (traditionalist, wary of speculation), and historically the Mu'tazila, who held that the Quran was created.

schools.name: Law
schools.text: Four Sunni schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) and the Ja'fari school of Twelver Shia Islam.

why_it_matters: When a Muslim friend says 'Islam teaches...', it is worth asking which source and which school. A verse of the Quran, an authentic hadith, a medieval commentator and a modern preacher carry very different weight within Islam itself. Answer the Islam your friend actually holds.
